question.text: In the Indian context, which of the following best explains the calendar-based anomaly observed in Jan-March of each financial year?

answer.text: Mutual funds aggressively buy stocks before year-end to window-dress NAVs, pushing prices UP sharply.
FPIs uniformly redeem during Jan-March due to RBI's debt-market rules.
SEBI mandates a trading halt for the last week of March, leading to price distortions.
Reduced liquidity from advance-tax outflows, bank/NBFC balance-sheet dressing, government borrowing and tax-loss harvesting (wash-sale-like booking) creates seasonal pressure on prices.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Ch 3.4.1, the last quarter (Jan-Mar) of the Indian FY is characterised by reduced liquidity: advance-tax payments, closing-transaction anticipation, government borrowing mop-up, bank/NBFC deposit-and-bond drives, and tax-loss-harvesting ('wash sales' equivalent). These are seasonal inefficiencies linked to the financial-year calendar. The Trap: Option A misstates direction (NAV dressing typically marginal and may go either way). Option B is a fabrication. Option C invents a non-existent SEBI halt. Cross-Exam Context: US literature documents the 'January Effect' (post-Dec tax selling rebound). XIX-C/XIX-A/XIX-B all touch calendar effects; XIX-C expects you to articulate the India-specific drivers. Manager's Pro-Tip: If your Cat III fund runs a Q4 India strategy, pre-communicate expected drawdown windows and liquidity tightness to LPs in quarterly letters - don't let LPs mistake seasonal beta drag for manager underperformance.
